row.basis: Moses receives words for his mission
row.note: The commentary connects Moses' prayer for a loosened tongue with the prophet's preparation to speak. In Exodus God answers Moses' speech fear by promising to be with his mouth and teach him what to say, making divine ease a concrete aid to prophetic speech.

row.basis: Moses names his slow speech
row.note: The commentary recalls Moses asking for his chest and tongue to be prepared before addressing Pharaoh. In Exodus Moses says he is slow of mouth and tongue during his call, giving the same figure a speech impediment that frames the later promise of help.

row.basis: God claims the making of the mouth
row.note: The commentary says the one who prepares the messenger also knows and equips the person within. In Exodus God answers Moses' limitation by asking who made the human mouth, grounding the messenger's capacity in the sender.

row.basis: The word near the mouth and heart
row.note: The commentary says revelation is made easy as the prophet's tongue becomes ready for the word. Moses says the command is near, in mouth and heart, so it can be done; both locate readiness in the person who receives and carries the word.

row.basis: The command is not too hard or far away
row.note: The commentary hears the unnamed easiest destination as a divine easing of the person. Deuteronomy describes its command as not too difficult or remote, an Israelite counterpart in which God's instruction is accessible for action.

row.basis: An enlarged heart makes the runner able
row.note: The commentary distinguishes smoothing a road from preparing its traveler. The psalmist says that when God enlarges his heart, he will run in the way of God's commandments; inner preparation enables swift movement along the way.

row.basis: A taught tongue sustains the weary
row.note: The commentary links an eased prophet to a tongue made ready for reminder. Isaiah's servant receives a trained tongue to sustain the weary and an awakened ear each morning, showing prophetic readiness as both listening and speech for others.

row.basis: God places words in the prophet's mouth
row.note: The commentary presents the reciting God as the source of a messenger's prepared speech. In Moses' promise of a prophet like him, God puts divine words in that prophet's mouth, specifying what being made ready to speak entails.

row.basis: A touched mouth receives God's words
row.note: The commentary describes the prophet himself as prepared for the work of reminder. At Jeremiah's call God touches his mouth and puts words there before appointing him to speak, a concrete scene of the messenger being readied rather than the task being simplified.

row.basis: The prophet must speak what God commands
row.note: The commentary says the prepared messenger is then sent to remind others. Deuteronomy makes the prophet responsible to speak God's commanded words, joining divine preparation to the work that follows.

row.basis: Words remain in the messenger's mouth
row.note: The commentary places ease between recitation and not forgetting. Isaiah's covenant promise says God's words placed in the mouth will not depart from the servant and descendants, adding lasting retention to the image of prepared speech.

row.basis: The prophet eats the scroll, then speaks
row.note: The commentary joins receiving recitation to becoming ready to remind others. Ezekiel is told to take the scroll into himself and then go speak God's words to Israel, presenting preparation as inwardly receiving the message before carrying it outward.

row.basis: A coal prepares Isaiah's lips for service
row.note: The commentary recalls Moses' wish for his tongue to be loosened and Muhammad's opened chest before a mission. Isaiah's lips are touched and his guilt removed before he is sent, making bodily preparation for prophetic speech visible.

row.basis: The prepared prophet answers the call
row.note: The commentary says easing does not end in rest but enables the messenger's work. After Isaiah's lips are cleansed, he volunteers to be sent when God asks who will go, linking preparation directly to renewed service.

row.basis: God guides the addressee with counsel
row.note: The commentary pairs a leader going ahead with a follower prepared to move easily. The psalm promises instruction and guidance with God's eye on the addressee, giving the leader-follower relation a personal form.

row.basis: A horse needs bit and bridle to be guided
row.note: The commentary's horse image is easy to direct with a light touch. The psalm warns that horse or mule without understanding must be restrained by bit and bridle, a pointed difference about whether the follower is already docile.

row.basis: Running and walking continue without fainting
row.note: The commentary says divine ease does not cancel the journey or let the messenger stop working. Isaiah promises that those who wait for the Lord will run without weariness and walk without fainting, sustaining movement through exertion.

row.basis: The shepherd goes ahead and the sheep follow his voice
row.note: The commentary develops a leader in front of a compliant follower who takes the road by its own steps. Jesus' shepherd goes ahead and the sheep follow because they know his voice, an especially close image of guided following.

row.basis: The Father's Spirit speaks through the messenger
row.note: The commentary says the prophet's tongue is prepared for the word rather than speaking ahead of it. Jesus tells disciples that the Spirit of their Father speaks through them under trial, locating their speech in divine aid.

row.basis: Words are given at the hour of testimony
row.note: The commentary reads ease as preparation of the person who must speak. Jesus tells disciples not to worry beforehand about what to say when handed over, because the words will be given then; readiness replaces anxious self-provision.

row.basis: The Spirit teaches and brings Jesus' words to memory
row.note: The commentary places the promise beside recitation, not forgetting, and later reminding. Jesus says the Spirit will teach the disciples and remind them of what he said, joining preparation of understanding to remembered speech.

row.basis: Paul reads Deuteronomy's near word as proclaimed faith
row.note: The commentary makes a prepared tongue the place where the received word becomes ready speech. Paul quotes Moses' word near the mouth and heart as the word of faith he proclaims, giving Deuteronomy's accessibility a Christian preaching interpretation.

row.basis: An easy yoke and light burden
row.note: The commentary says the load need not disappear for the walk to become easier. Jesus calls his yoke easy and burden light, giving a direct Christian image of carrying an obligation under eased conditions.

row.basis: Gentleness accompanies taking the yoke
row.note: The commentary notes that easing another can mean treating that person gently, alongside preparing the traveler. Jesus calls himself gentle and humble in heart and invites disciples to learn from him under a yoke, linking gentleness with instruction.

row.basis: Jesus offers rest to the burdened
row.note: The commentary insists that ease for the messenger is not a rest: after the work, he is told to take up the next task. Jesus invites the weary and burdened to come for rest, making the contrast in what ease promises explicit.

row.basis: Wisdom's yoke is taken up for instruction
row.note: The commentary portrays the prophet as prepared to bear a continuing task. Ben Sira urges the learner to put the neck under Wisdom's yoke and receive instruction, a Jewish wisdom picture of accepting disciplined service.

row.basis: Labor leads to much rest in Wisdom
row.note: The commentary says ease does not mean rest but makes renewed work possible. Ben Sira says he labored little and found much rest in Wisdom, setting a wisdom-seeking outcome beside the commentary's continuing prophetic labor.

row.basis: The Torah's yoke displaces worldly burdens
row.note: The commentary says the messenger's work remains, though he is made able to carry it. The Mishnah teaches that taking Torah's yoke removes the yoke of worldly concerns, a Jewish account of religious obligation changing how other burdens are borne.

row.basis: Run the appointed race after laying aside weight
row.note: The commentary's light-footed traveler still keeps moving and takes up the next task. Hebrews tells runners to lay aside every weight and run with endurance the race set before them, joining bodily lightness to sustained service.

row.basis: Straight paths are made for weakened feet
row.note: The commentary stresses that the ayah prepares the traveler while leaving the road as it is. Hebrews tells the community to make straight paths for its feet so the lame may be healed, a complementary reversal in which the path is adjusted for the weak.

row.basis: The easy road leads to destruction
row.note: The commentary associates the easiest destination with God's favor and contrasts it with the hardest way. Jesus says the broad, easy road leads to destruction, directly reversing the moral value attached to ease.

row.basis: The hard way leads to life
row.note: The commentary reads divine preparation toward the easiest as a good gift. Jesus says the narrow, difficult way leads to life and few find it, making difficulty rather than ease the mark of the saving route.

row.basis: God's commandments are not burdensome
row.note: The commentary presents the person as made ready for a task rather than freed from it. First John says God's commandments are not burdensome for those who love God, a Christian ethical formulation of obedience made bearable.

row.basis: Open the hand to the poor despite scarcity
row.note: The commentary says material ease is not itself the promised good and points instead to the person who gives. Deuteronomy commands an open hand and a loan to the needy, placing generosity rather than retained wealth at the center of faithful action.

row.basis: Give without a grudging heart
row.note: The commentary describes the person made easy for the good path as one who gives wealth away. Deuteronomy says to give freely and not resent it, connecting inward readiness with concrete generosity.

row.basis: The rich man promises himself ease and rest
row.note: The commentary separates spiritual ease from wealth and from resting after labor. In Jesus' parable the rich man tells himself to take ease, eat, drink, and be merry because of his stores, showing the false security of material abundance.

row.basis: Stored wealth cannot protect the rich fool from death
row.note: The commentary says a person's money will not help when he falls and that worldly ease can prepare one for hardship. In the parable God demands the rich man's life that night, exposing the failure of his possessions to secure his future.

row.basis: Being rich toward God differs from storing for oneself
row.note: The commentary contrasts the giver with the person who counts himself self-sufficient. Jesus concludes that one who stores treasure for himself but is not rich toward God has misunderstood prosperity, sharpening the same ethical contrast.

row.basis: The lot's decision belongs to the Lord
row.note: The commentary contrasts meysir's chance allocation with the divine speaker who measures and prepares a person. Proverbs says a lot is cast but its decision is from the Lord, a direct counter-reading of lots as mere chance.

row.basis: Lots assign the two goats for the atonement rite
row.note: The commentary treats the camel-share game as condemned chance-taking. Leviticus uses lots to distinguish the goat for the Lord from the goat for Azazel, showing an Israelite ritual use of lots with sacred, ordered ends.

row.basis: Land is apportioned by lot before the Lord
row.note: The commentary contrasts shares left to drawn arrows with a divinely measured portion. Joshua casts lots at Shiloh before the Lord to distribute the land among Israel's clans, making allotment a public sacred act rather than gambling.

row.basis: The high priest draws lots for the goats
row.note: The commentary's meysir scene has arrows determine shares of a slaughtered animal. The Mishnah describes the high priest drawing lots between the goats for the Temple rite, a Jewish ritual counterpart that distinguishes sacred selection from a game of gain.

row.basis: A lot selects Matthias for apostolic service
row.note: The commentary contrasts arbitrary shares with a person prepared by God's agency. Acts reports that the community casts a lot to select Matthias for the apostolic office, a Christian use of lot to assign a vocation rather than divide winnings.

row.basis: Jesus' easy yoke is joined to gentle lordship
row.note: The commentary hears ease as both preparation and gentle treatment. This apocryphal Jesus saying joins an easy yoke to a gentle lordship, giving the gentleness implicit in the commentary's Arabic usage a distinct Christian witness; it also promises rest, which the commentary withholds.

row.basis: Rabbinic reading of Deuteronomy's accessible Torah
row.note: The commentary interprets ease as the messenger being made ready for the work. The Talmud reads Deuteronomy's word as neither in heaven nor across the sea but accessible to the learner, shifting the parallel from prophetic aptitude to the effort of Torah study.

row.basis: The Torah is no longer adjudicated in heaven
row.note: The commentary stresses that the divine "we" supplies and prepares the prophetic word. In the Oven of Akhnai story, rabbis invoke Deuteronomy's "not in heaven" to place legal interpretation with human sages, a contrasting Jewish account of who governs revealed speech.

row.basis: Affliction is light while apostolic work continues
row.note: The commentary says hardship is not erased, but the burden is made carryable and the messenger keeps working. Paul calls present affliction light in view of eternal glory, placing enduring labor and a changed measure of weight together.

row.basis: God knows a word before it reaches the tongue
row.note: The commentary says the one who eases the prophet knows what is hidden within him. The psalm says God knows the speaker's word before it is on his tongue, joining inward knowledge to speech before utterance.

row.basis: God's Spirit causes the people to walk in the statutes
row.note: The commentary's central distinction is that the traveler is made ready, not merely given a smoother road. Ezekiel promises God's Spirit within the people will cause them to walk in God's statutes, directly locating readiness in the walkers.

row.basis: A voice commands that the Lord's way be prepared
row.note: The commentary stresses that the ayah makes the person easy while the road remains. Isaiah instead commands preparation of the Lord's way in the wilderness, a precise contrast in what is readied.

row.basis: Valleys are raised and rough ground made level
row.note: The commentary says ease can be placed in the traveler's gait even when the route is difficult. Isaiah pictures the route itself being leveled, so the shared journey image makes the different means of easing clear.

row.basis: Luke applies Isaiah's prepared-way voice to John
row.note: The commentary contrasts preparing the traveler with smoothing the path. Luke quotes Isaiah's command to prepare the Lord's way as the setting for John the Baptist's preaching, making the voice of a prophet the means of preparing a route.

row.basis: Wisdom's instruction keeps the walk and run unhindered
row.note: The commentary says the messenger is made light-footed and ready for the way. Proverbs says the instructed person's step will not be hampered when walking or stumbling when running, linking guidance with unhindered movement.

row.basis: God gives the speaker a deer's feet for the heights
row.note: The commentary develops the image of a responsive mount with light legs that carries its rider over a route. The psalm says God makes the speaker's feet like a deer's and sets him on the heights, a close image of divinely enabled movement.

row.basis: God widens the space beneath the speaker's steps
row.note: The commentary says the road stays as it is while the traveler is made ready. The psalm credits God with widening the speaker's steps so his feet do not slip, bringing the contrasting image of the route itself made spacious.

row.basis: God gives deer-like feet on high places amid scarcity
row.note: The commentary's light-footed traveler can keep moving even when the route is steep. Habakkuk says God makes his feet like a deer's and enables him to tread on heights, in a passage that names famine and crop failure immediately before this trust.

row.basis: The messenger's feet carry news of peace and salvation
row.note: The commentary brings together the prophet's reminder and the image of light steps on a route. Isaiah praises the feet of the messenger who announces peace and salvation, joining movement to the work of proclamation.

row.basis: Paul applies Isaiah's beautiful feet to gospel proclamation
row.note: The commentary's prepared messenger is enabled to carry a reminder. Paul quotes Isaiah's messenger with beautiful feet to explain the sending of Christian preachers, giving the older restoration image an apostolic preaching interpretation.

row.basis: God equips the community to do God's will
row.note: The commentary reads ease as preparation of the person for continuing work. Hebrews asks God to equip the community with everything good for doing God's will and to work within them, a direct Christian formulation of inwardly enabled service.

row.basis: A cleansed vessel is prepared for every good work
row.note: The commentary hears “we will make you easy” as “we will prepare you” for the assigned task. Second Timothy describes a person as a vessel prepared for every good work, giving that secondary sense a concrete Christian counterpart.

row.basis: The good works are prepared for the believer to walk in
row.note: The commentary emphasizes that the prophet himself is the direct object of preparation. Ephesians says God prepared the good works beforehand for believers to walk in, shifting preparation from the person to the course of action.

row.basis: The Lord who knows hearts is asked to choose a messenger
row.note: The commentary connects the promise of ease with the speaker's knowledge of what is hidden in a person. Before a lot selects an apostle, Acts addresses the Lord as the one who knows everyone's heart and asks him to show whom he has chosen.

row.basis: The Spirit gives the utterance that the disciples speak
row.note: The commentary says the messenger receives and follows a recitation supplied by God. At Pentecost the disciples speak as the Spirit gives them utterance, extending divinely enabled speech from one prophet to a gathered community.

row.basis: Soldiers cast lots to divide Jesus' garment
row.note: The commentary describes meysir as a game in which arrows assign portions of a slaughtered camel. John depicts soldiers using lots to divide Jesus' clothing, a concrete scene of chance allocation presented as an act of humiliation.

row.basis: The lot identifies Jonathan in a crisis
row.note: The commentary distinguishes gambling for shares from an outcome assigned by divine measure. Saul's lot falls on Jonathan while the people seek the cause of a military crisis, showing lots used to identify responsibility rather than to win a game.
